title: USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino not waiting to work the refs
content:
Get free access to the most comprehensive World Cup coverage in the app, from kickoff to the trophy lift.

CHICAGO — Whether it’s a long-term frustration that boiled over Saturday or perhaps a bit of gamesmanship toward referees ahead of the World Cup, U.S. national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino isn’t happy about the whistle his team is getting.

The United States fell to Germany 2-1 at Soldier Field in its final pre-World Cup friendly, and things got tense deep in second-half stoppage time. For Pochettino, his irritations had been building not only throughout the game but also throughout his tenure as USMNT head coach.

“For 1 1/2 years, every time we play games, it’s like the referee always forgets we are the United States,” Pochettino said.

In stoppage time Saturday, winger Tim Weah was on the receiving end of a tough challenge or two, so he returned the favor and delivered a clean — but hard — slide tackle in the dying moments of the friendly.

The German players didn’t take that too kindly, with minutes separating them from their own World Cup journey. This is a team that lost Lennart Karl from the roster due to injury this week. It didn’t want to risk another.

Weah didn’t back down. German defender Nico Schlotterbeck approached Weah angrily. Weston McKennie got off the bench to defend his guy and yelled back. Sebastian Berhalter and Cristian Roldan quickly came to Weah’s defense, too. German defenders Jonathan Tah and Waldemar Anton got involved.

Angry words and maybe a shove or two were exchanged before cooler heads prevailed, with Pochettino himself arriving to separate the players.

“Germany was a little more aggressive from the beginning, and I think the referee didn’t manage the situation well,” Pochettino said. “It created the feeling like, OK, we need to be aggressive, too, like this.”

Pochettino’s frustrations might have merit.

In the fall, friendly matches against Paraguay and Australia were quite physical. Coincidentally, all three nations were drawn in Group D together at the World Cup with Turkey, another recent USMNT opponent, the fourth.

The Paraguay game ended with a fracas. A physical game, in which the USMNT was called for 13 fouls to Paraguay’s 11, ended in a near fight. A disagreement over a throw-in resulted in Gustavo Gómez and Alex Freeman wrestling for the ball, and then Berhalter intervened. So did Miles Robinson, who was swiftly put in a headlock by a Paraguayan player.

Pochettino ran over to try to calm the situation and slipped around the throng of bodies, which he later called a “very, very dangerous situation.”

The Australia game was marred by the deliberately physical treatment of USMNT star Christian Pulisic. He was substituted in the first half due to injury, after several challenges.

The final one was made by Australia’s Jason Geria, who said he wasn’t trying to injure anybody but acknowledged “there were physical battles everywhere.”

That game, too, saw the USMNT called for more fouls (16) than its opponent (10).

The USMNT is unlikely to forget these two situations ahead of its first two group-stage matches, against the same opponents. Maybe it was already on Pochettino’s mind in his news conference Saturday. Maybe it’s one way of already working the World Cup refs.

Pochettino tried to work the refs Saturday, too. He even noted it was convenient that the referee in the game against Germany was Chilean, so it was a bit easier to speak in Spanish, Pochettino’s first language.

Against Paraguay on Friday, the referee won’t be Chilean, because referees at the World Cup cannot be from the same federation as either team playing. Pochettino won’t know who the ref will be, either, as they are not officially confirmed and assigned until 24 to 48 hours before a match.

There is an art form to working the referee or operating right on the line of what is or isn’t acceptable in a given game. In South America and Concacaf, it’s often referred to as the dark arts of soccer. Though off-ball cheap shots can no longer go unpunished in the era of the video assistant referee system, finding the line from any given refereeing crew and using it to your advantage remains a skill.

Coaches knowing how much to complain or criticize, when to yell or when a more diplomatic approach is warranted is all part of it. And at this tournament, where legacies are on the line and the margins are so thin, there is no advantage too small to pursue.

No matter what, physicality is not just part of the game but a trait of all the great U.S. men’s national teams of the past. Whether it was Alexi Lalas in World Cups in 1994 and 1998 or Oguchi Onyewu in 2006 and 2010, Geoff Cameron in 2014, Walker Zimmerman in 2022, Michael Bradley or Tyler Adams at the heart of midfield from 2010 to now, and everybody in between, it is a staple of this program.

The players appreciate it, too. In the aforementioned games against Paraguay and Australia, anyone speaking to the media after the matches echoed a similar sentiment: We’ve got one another’s backs no matter what, and we won’t get bullied.

“It shows that guys are in it, willing to protect each other, wanting to get involved,” USMNT captain Tim Ream said after the Paraguay game. “Make sure we’re not going to be pushed around. … It’s a point of pride.”

Pochettino himself understands. An Argentine international center back during his playing days, he was aggressive and rugged.

Now, he’s being a little more diplomatic in trying to have referees see things his way. For now, at least.
